sense: the means: how something is done

terms.grammar: construction: the means in the ablative, with no preposition
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.105: mēns discendō alitur et cōgitandō
terms.comment: The ordinary way: pedibus, on foot; manū, by hand; litterīs, by letter. “By doing” is the ablative of the gerund: ambulandō, by walking. A person who does it takes ā (see “by”, the doer); a person through whom it is done takes per. For “thanks to”, see due to.

terms.gloss: through, by means of (a go-between, a channel)
evidence: Caes. BG 1.12.2: per explōrātōrēs Caesar certior factus est
Cic. Att. 4.14.1: mē per litterās fēcit certiōrem
terms.comment: Chiefly of the person who carries a thing out or brings word, and of channels such as per litterās.

phrases.latin: Actiō māluimus iter facere pedibus quī incommodissimē nāvigāssēmus
phrases.english: from Actium we preferred to travel on foot, after a most uncomfortable voyage

phrases.latin: multae etiam istārum arborum meā manū sunt satae
phrases.english: many of these trees were even planted by my own hand

phrases.latin: hominis autem mēns discendō alitur et cōgitandō
phrases.english: the human mind is fed by learning and thinking

phrases.latin: Sōcratēn ferunt, cum ūsque ad vesperum contentius ambulāret quaesītumque esset ex eō quārē id faceret, respondisse sē, quō melius cēnāret, obsōnāre ambulandō famem
phrases.english: they say that Socrates, walking hard until evening and asked why he did it, answered that by walking he was buying in hunger, to enjoy his dinner more

phrases.latin: Ubi per explōrātōrēs Caesar certior factus est trēs jam partēs cōpiārum Helvētiōs id flūmen trādūxisse
phrases.english: when Caesar learned through his scouts that the Helvetii had already taken three quarters of their forces across that river
